events.title: First commercial blade servers ship
events.summary: RLX Technologies began shipping the first commercial blade servers in June 2001 — ultra-dense x86 servers in a shared chassis.
events.about: Blade servers swapped standalone 1U boxes for interchangeable cards sharing power, cooling, and networking in a chassis — HP, [IBM], and Dell followed with c-Class, BladeCenter, and PowerEdge blades. Datacenters packed more compute per rack for virtualization hosts and web tiers. Backend developers deploying on "blades" in the 2000s ran on this form factor.

narrative.whyChosen: RLX blade servers pioneered the dense datacenter form factor that dominated 2000s enterprise hosting.
narrative.whyImportant: Blades made horizontal scaling cheaper and standardized rack infrastructure for virtualization.
narrative.problemSolved: Traditional rack servers wasted space, power, and cabling in growing datacenters.

events.title: Nokia 9210 Communicator released
events.summary: Nokia released the Nokia 9210 Communicator in June 2001 — a color-screen [Symbian] Communicator with a fold-out QWERTY keyboard.
events.about: Nokia hardware shaped pre-iPhone smartphones and later Microsoft's mobile platform bet. Color screen symbian communicator with fold-out qwerty keyboard.

narrative.whyChosen: The Nokia 9210 Communicator was a flagship Nokia smartphone milestone.
narrative.whyImportant: Nokia devices defined mobile platforms from [Symbian] through Windows Phone.
narrative.problemSolved: Mobile users needed capable smartphones before the iPhone/[Android] era matured.

events.title: Steve Ballmer calls Linux "a cancer"
events.summary: In a Chicago Sun-Times interview, Microsoft CEO Steve Ballmer attacks the [GPL] and open-source licensing.
events.about: Ballmer was arguing that [copyleft] 'infects' proprietary code — a framing open-source advocates still push back on. The quote marked peak Microsoft–Linux hostility before Azure embraced open source.

narrative.whyChosen: The most inflammatory corporate quote of the open-source wars.
narrative.whyImportant: It galvanized the free-software community and defined Microsoft's public stance for years.
narrative.problemSolved: Microsoft was defending its licensing model against government open-source adoption.

events.quoteText: Linux is a cancer that attaches itself in an intellectual property sense to everything it touches.
